explication:
<explanation>
1. Identify the project type and purpose  
   - This is a content-driven static site (a “Jamstack” site) that powers GitHub’s community-curated Topics and Collections pages.  
   - It uses Markdown files under `topics/` and `collections/` plus Jekyll/Liquid templates to generate a static website.  

2. Analyze the file structure  
   - Top-level content:  
     • `topics/` (folder full of `<topic>/index.md`)  
     • `collections/` (folder full of `<collection>/index.md`)  
   - Site engine/configuration:  
     • `_config.yml` – Jekyll configuration  
     • `feed.json.liquid` – Liquid template for feeds  
     • `Rakefile` – build tasks  
   - Tooling/development:  
     • `Gemfile`/`Gemfile.lock` – Ruby dependencies (Jekyll, plugins, rubocop)  
     • `.github/workflows/` – CI workflows (jekyll_build, lint, test, etc.)  
     • `test/` – Ruby‐based lint/format checks  
   - Deployment:  
     • `CNAME` – custom domain for GitHub Pages  
     • GitHub Pages picks up the `main` (or `gh-pages`) branch  

3. Examine the README for additional insights  
   - Describes that tests/lint run via GitHub Actions and locally with `bundle exec rubocop`.  
   - Mentions that content is under CC-BY-4.0 and contributions follow CONTRIBUTING.md.  

4. Main components & relationships — diagram outline  
   A. Developer Environment  
     - Code editor + local Ruby/Bundler  
     - Markdown content + Jekyll templates  
     - `bundle exec jekyll serve` for local preview  
   B. GitHub Repository (central source)  
     - Stores all Markdown, config, templates, CI definitions  
   C. Continuous Integration (GitHub Actions)  
     1. Lint & tests (`lint.yml`, `test.yml`)  
     2. Build (`jekyll_build.yml`) – runs Jekyll to generate HTML  
   D. Artifact Deployment  
     - Upon successful build, GitHub Pages deploys `_site/` to the public endpoint  
   E. Hosting (GitHub Pages/CDN)  
     - Static HTML/CSS/JS served via GitHub’s CDN under the custom domain in `CNAME`  

5. Architectural patterns & design principles  
   - Jamstack static site pattern:  
     • Content as data (Markdown)  
     • Build time rendering (Jekyll)  
     • CDN deployment (GitHub Pages)  
   - Clear separation of concerns:  
     • Content (topics/collections)  
     • Presentation (templates, `_config.yml`)  
     • Build pipeline (Rake tasks, GitHub Actions)  
     • Enforcement (Rubocop, tests)  
   - Extensibility point: add new `topics/<name>/index.md` or collections, and push changes  

6. Technologies, frameworks, libraries  
   - Ruby & Bundler (dependency management)  
   - Jekyll (static site generator) + Liquid templates  
   - GitHub Actions (CI/CD workflows)  
   - Rubocop + custom tests (linting/formatting)  
   - GitHub Pages (hosting)  

7. Diagram-drawing guidelines  
   a. Components/Shapes  
     - Use rectangular boxes for “actors” and “systems”  
     - Use cylinder shape for any data store or repository (though here source is a Git repo)  
     - Group related items (e.g., Developer Tools, CI Pipeline) using dashed containers  
   b. Arrows & data flow  
     - Developer → GitHub Repo (push / pull request)  
     - Repo → GitHub Actions (trigger workflows)  
     - Actions → Lint/Test → Build → Artifacts  
     - Artifacts → GitHub Pages → Users (HTTP GET requests)  
   c. Color coding  
     - Blue: Source content & repo  
     - Orange: CI workflow  
     - Green: Build engine (Jekyll)  
     - Purple: Hosting/CDN  
   d. Labels  
     - Clearly label each arrow (e.g., “PR triggers lint/test”, “Build generates HTML”)  
     - Label each box with component name and key technology (e.g., “Jekyll Build Server (Ruby, Liquid)”)  

8. Tailor to this static-site project  
   - Emphasize Markdown source → Jekyll build → static assets → GitHub Pages hosting.  
   - Highlight CI gates: rubocop linting, topic/collection formatting tests, Jekyll build errors.  
   - Show how a new topic or collection flows from contributor proposal to live page.  

9. Be very detailed  
   - Include all workflows under `.github/workflows` as separate CI steps.  
   - Show dependency on `Gemfile` and external plugins.  
   - Capture that `CNAME` config maps to a custom domain.  

By following these steps and using clear labels, directional arrows, color-coding, and grouping, you will create a precise, comprehensive system design diagram for the GitHub Explore static site project.  
</explanation>
